RFC 7516 (JSON Web Encryption) scoped to github.com/iscultas/jwt-go, which implements JWE in the jwe package and wires it into the JWT layer: all six RFC 7518 section 5 content encryption algorithms, all sixteen section 4 key management algorithms, both JSON serializations and the compact one, multi-recipient messages, and Nested JWTs.

Three deliberate narrowings are recorded against individual requirements rather than left implicit, because each is a place this module refuses something RFC 7516 permits:

(1) RSA1_5 decrypts and never encrypts, and is not among the algorithms jwt.DefaultDecryptionConfig accepts. RFC 7518 section 4.1 marks it Recommended-, and RFC 8725 section 3.2 -- a BCP that formally updates RFC 7519 -- asks applications to avoid all RSA-PKCS1 v1.5 encryption algorithms, preferring RSAES-OAEP. It was unimplemented here until the two costs of that position came due: RFC 7519 section 8 states an unqualified MUST for it (RFC7519-S8-R05), and Appendix A.2, one recipient of Appendix A.4, RFC 7520 section 5.1 and one recipient of RFC 7520 section 5.13 were all unreadable. The decrypting half is implemented now, which meets both documents: the algorithm exists, and neither a producer nor a default consumer reaches it. What makes that safe is section 11.5's own recommendation, a substituted random CEK in place of a padding error, which this module implements for RSA1_5 and for no other algorithm. See RFC7516-S11_4-R01, RFC7516-S11_5-R01 and RFC8725-S3_2-R06.

(2) The "enc" Header Parameter is read from the JWE Protected Header alone, and "alg" from a per-recipient header only when the protected header names none. RFC 7516 section 7.2.1 would allow either anywhere. Outside the protected header a parameter is outside the Additional Authenticated Data and can be rewritten in transit, which is the algorithm confusion of RFC 8725 section 3.1; the asymmetry between the two is argued at RFC7516-S7_2_1-R15 and at jwe.keyManagement. It is why RFC 7520 sections 5.11 to 5.13 stay excluded from the interop suite.

(3) "zip" is decompressed on the way in but never produced on the way out, per RFC 8725 section 3.6's SHOULD NOT. Both directions are asserted -- RFC7516-S4_1_3-R03 and -R04 -- since the asymmetry is the behaviour, not an omission.

Sections defined wholly by reference to RFC 7515 -- 4.1.1 and 4.1.4 through 4.1.13, 5.3, 6 -- are recorded in `sections` with a cross-reference to the RFC 7515 requirement ids that own them, rather than enriched here. The header type is shared between jws and jwe, so duplicating those requirements would double-count the same assertions against the same code. Section 8 (TLS) has no surface: this module dereferences no URL. Section 10 is registry procedure.

Six requirements carry no BCP 14 keyword and were added during enrichment rather than found by the extractor, per RFC 8174 section 2: the compact serialization grammar (7.1), the three rules for distinguishing a JWS from a JWE (9), the Additional Authenticated Data computation (5.1 step 14), and the chosen-ciphertext countermeasure (11.4). Each is wire format or security-critical behaviour that a keyword scan simply does not reach.

Errata reviewed: 6018 (editorial, "initialization vector" for "initialization value" -- terminology only), 7719 (section 6, key identification and AEAD key commitment -- recorded against that section, since the reporter's point is sound and the RFC's stated justification is weaker than it reads), and 8676 (section 5.2 step 14, recomputing the Encoded Protected Header -- this module already uses the octets a header arrived as rather than a re-serialization, which is the behaviour the erratum asks for; see RFC7516-S5_1-R02).

source.text: These JSON data structures MAY contain whitespace and/or line breaks before or after any JSON values or structural characters, in accordance with Section 2 of RFC 7159 [RFC7159].

requirements.condition: reading a JWE JSON Serialization that carries whitespace or line breaks around values or structural characters
requirements.behavior: accept it, since RFC 7159 permits insignificant whitespace
requirements.observable_effect: a pretty-printed JWE JSON document decodes and decrypts to the same plaintext as its compact form
requirements.oracle: json.MarshalIndent applied to a jwe.Message's JSON serialization, then decoded through (*jwe.Message).UnmarshalJSON and decrypted, yields the original plaintext. Verified empirically before this oracle was written. The permission is exercised by producers, so the obligation this suite can assert is the receiving half: a document another implementation formatted must still be readable. Note that the whitespace tolerance stops at the base64url parts -- RFC 7516 section 5.2 step 2 forbids line breaks or whitespace inside those, which is a separate requirement.
inputs: a JWE JSON Serialization indented with json.MarshalIndent

notes: contains a conditional; capture the guard in `condition` rather than in `behavior`

source.text: In the JWE JSON Serialization, one or more of the JWE Protected Header, JWE Shared Unprotected Header, and JWE Per-Recipient Unprotected Header MUST be present.

requirements.condition: producing or consuming a JWE JSON Serialization
requirements.behavior: ensure at least one of the JWE Protected Header, JWE Shared Unprotected Header and JWE Per-Recipient Unprotected Header is present
requirements.observable_effect: a message with no header at all is refused rather than decrypted
requirements.oracle: A jwe.Message whose ProtectedHeader is nil fails with jwe.ErrMalformedMessage on both Encrypt and Decrypt. This module is stricter than the RFC here and the difference is recorded rather than hidden: RFC 7516 would allow the sole header to be an unprotected one, but jwe.contentEncryption requires a protected header because "enc" is read from it alone -- see RFC7516-S7_2_1-R15 for that argument. The requirement as stated is therefore satisfied a fortiori: this package refuses everything the RFC refuses, and some of what it permits.
inputs: a message with no headers at all
open_questions: A JWE whose only header is unprotected is legal per RFC 7516 but is refused here. That narrowing is argued at jwe.contentEncryption and is the same one behind excluding RFC 7520 sections 5.11 to 5.13 from the interop suite.

source.text: The inclusion of some of these values is OPTIONAL.

requirements.condition: producing a JWE JSON Serialization
requirements.behavior: omit the members whose values are absent rather than writing them empty
requirements.observable_effect: a message with no shared header, no per-recipient header and no aad serializes without the "unprotected", "header" and "aad" members
requirements.oracle: json.Marshal of a single-recipient jwe.Message built with none of the optional values produces an object whose members are exactly "protected", "encrypted_key", "iv", "ciphertext" and "tag". The optional ones are absent rather than present-and-empty, which RFC 7516 section 7.2.1 requires member by member and which this requirement states in summary.
inputs: a minimal single-recipient message

notes: short REQUIRED/OPTIONAL usage; often a field-table label rather than a requirement

source.text: The Header Parameter names within the JOSE Header MUST be unique, just as described in Section 4 of [JWS].

requirements.condition: parsing a JOSE Header JSON object that repeats a member name
requirements.behavior: either reject it or resolve it the way Section 4 of RFC 7515 permits; this implementation rejects
requirements.observable_effect: a header repeating a name is refused, deterministically
requirements.oracle: Decoding base64url({"alg":"A128KW","enc":"A128GCM","kid":"one","kid":"two"}) through (*header.Header).Unmarshal returns an error for which errors.Is(err, jsontext.ErrDuplicateName) holds. Verified empirically. RFC 7516 incorporates RFC 7515 section 4 by reference ("just as described in Section 4 of [JWS]"), and that section offers two conforming behaviours: reject, or use a parser returning only the lexically last member. This implementation takes the first, on the JWE path exactly as on the JWS path.
inputs: a protected header repeating kid

source.text: This algorithm MUST be an AEAD algorithm with a specified key length.

requirements.condition: resolving an "enc" Header Parameter value
requirements.behavior: accept only algorithms that provide authenticated encryption with associated data and a fixed key length
requirements.observable_effect: every registered enc algorithm returns an authentication tag and reports a single valid CEK length; no other algorithm resolves as an enc
requirements.oracle: For each of the six algorithms this module registers as jwa.ContentEncrypter, Encrypt returns a non-empty tag alongside the ciphertext, Decrypt with any altered tag returns jwa.ErrDecryptionFailed, and KeySize returns a fixed positive value that a CEK of any other length is refused against with jwa.ErrInvalidKeySize. Conversely, resolving a signature algorithm name such as "HS256" as an enc fails: header.Header's EncryptionAlgorithm field is typed jwa.ContentEncrypter, so a name that resolves to something else is refused where it is read.
inputs: each registered enc algorithm
"HS256" offered as an enc

source.text: This Header Parameter MUST be present and MUST be understood and processed by implementations.

requirements.condition: reading or producing any JWE
requirements.behavior: require the "enc" Header Parameter to be present and process it
requirements.observable_effect: a JWE whose headers name no enc is refused rather than defaulted

compound_review.rationale: presence and processing are one obligation on the receiver, and the oracle asserts both: nothing is defaulted and nothing falls back

requirements.oracle: jwe.Message.Encrypt and Decrypt both return jwe.ErrMalformedMessage when the protected header's EncryptionAlgorithm is nil. Nothing is defaulted: there is no fallback enc anywhere in the package, which is what "MUST be present" requires of a consumer that cannot ask for one.
inputs: a message whose protected header names alg but not enc

source.text: Other values MAY be used.

requirements.condition: a "zip" value other than "DEF" is encountered
requirements.behavior: the permission to define other values exists; an implementation that does not support one must not silently ignore it
requirements.observable_effect: a JWE naming a zip other than "DEF" is refused rather than decrypted uncompressed
requirements.oracle: Decrypting a message whose protected header carries zip:"XYZ" returns an error rather than the compressed octets passed through unchanged. This is the interop half of a MAY and is not skipped: the capability is absent here, and the obligation on an implementation lacking it is to refuse, since treating an unknown compression as no compression would emit octets that are not the plaintext.
inputs: a protected header with zip:"XYZ"

source.text: When used, this Header Parameter MUST be integrity protected; therefore, it MUST occur only within the

requirements.condition: a "zip" Header Parameter is present
requirements.behavior: read it only from the JWE Protected Header, so that it is integrity protected
requirements.observable_effect: a zip in the shared or per-recipient unprotected header has no effect on decryption

compound_review.rationale: the second MUST is the stated consequence of the first -- 'therefore' -- rather than an independent obligation

requirements.oracle: jwe.Message.decompress reads message.ProtectedHeader.CompressionAlgorithm and nothing else. A message whose protected header names no zip but whose shared or per-recipient header does is decrypted without decompression, and the recovered octets are the plaintext exactly as encrypted. Verified empirically. The rule matters because zip sits outside the AAD in those headers: an attacker who could add one would make the recipient inflate attacker-chosen octets, which is the decompression bomb ErrOversizedPlaintext bounds.
inputs: a message with zip in the shared unprotected header
the same in a per-recipient header

notes: contains a conditional; capture the guard in `condition` rather than in `behavior`

source.text: Use of this Header Parameter is OPTIONAL.

requirements.condition: producing a JWE
requirements.behavior: omit "zip" -- its use is optional
requirements.observable_effect: no JWE this module produces carries a zip parameter, and asking for one is refused
requirements.oracle: jwe.Message.Encrypt returns jwe.ErrCompressedPlaintext when the protected header names any zip. The permission is exercised by declining it, which is conformant: RFC 7516 makes use of the parameter OPTIONAL. The reason for declining is RFC 8725 section 3.6, and it is a SHOULD NOT rather than a MUST NOT, so the refusal is this module's choice and is recorded as one. See RFC8725-S3_6-R01.
inputs: a protected header requesting DEF

notes: short REQUIRED/OPTIONAL usage; often a field-table label rather than a requirement

source.text: This Header Parameter MUST be understood and processed by implementations.

requirements.condition: a "zip" Header Parameter of "DEF" is present on a JWE being decrypted
requirements.behavior: understand and process it -- decompress the plaintext
requirements.observable_effect: a compressed JWE from another implementation decrypts to the uncompressed plaintext
requirements.oracle: A JWE whose protected header carries zip:"DEF" and whose plaintext was raw-DEFLATE compressed decrypts to the original octets, bounded at 16 MiB. This is the direction the module does implement, and the asymmetry with RFC7516-S4_1_3-R03 is deliberate: refuse to write what you are willing to read. The RFC 7520 section 5.9 vector is the interop evidence.
inputs: a DEF-compressed JWE
RFC 7520 section 5.9

source.text: The CEK MUST have a length equal to that required for the content encryption algorithm.

requirements.condition: generating a CEK when Key Wrapping, Key Encryption or Key Agreement with Key Wrapping is employed
requirements.behavior: make it exactly the length the "enc" algorithm requires
requirements.observable_effect: every generated CEK is enc.KeySize() octets, for every pairing of alg and enc
requirements.oracle: jwa.GenerateContentEncryptionKey draws exactly encryption.KeySize() octets, and every wrapping algorithm's EncryptKey routes through it. Asserted across the full cross product of key management and content encryption algorithms rather than one pairing, since alg and enc are chosen independently and the CEK length is the only thing coupling them -- an algorithm that assumed one length would pass any single-pairing test.
inputs: every alg and enc pairing

source.text: However, in all cases, the encrypted content for at least one recipient MUST successfully validate or the JWE MUST be considered invalid.

requirements.condition: decrypting a JWE addressed to several recipients
requirements.behavior: consider the JWE invalid unless the encrypted content for at least one recipient validates
requirements.observable_effect: a message none of whose recipients validate returns an error and no plaintext

compound_review.rationale: one rule in two branches: the content for at least one recipient validates, or the JWE is invalid

requirements.oracle: jwe.Message.Decrypt tries every recipient in turn and returns jwa.ErrDecryptionFailed with a nil plaintext when none succeeds. Two cases are asserted, and the pair is the point. Appendix A.4 with its first recipient's "alg" rewritten to a name no registry holds, and its second recipient removed, is the "no recipient succeeded" case and fails (TestAMessageWithNoServiceableRecipientIsInvalid); the same rewritten document with both recipients is not, and decrypts with the second recipient's key (TestARecipientWeCannotServeDoesNotInvalidateTheMessage). The rewrite became necessary when RSA1_5 was implemented: every algorithm RFC 7518 section 4.1 registers is implemented now, so the published vector no longer carries a recipient this module cannot serve, though a producer using an algorithm a consumer lacks is the case step 18 exists for. The sentence is a floor on how many recipients must validate, not a ceiling: one is enough, and how many an application requires above that is left to the application, as the paragraph says. The single-recipient failure reports the unsupported algorithm as itself rather than collapsing to ErrDecryptionFailed -- with one recipient it is unambiguous whose algorithm was refused, and an attacker chooses none of it, so section 11.5 is not engaged.
inputs: Appendix A.4 rewritten to carry one recipient this module cannot serve
RFC 7516 Appendix A.4 with the A128KW recipient's key
a two-recipient message and a third party's key

source.text: When using the JWE JSON Serialization, this restriction includes that the same Header Parameter name also MUST NOT occur in distinct JSON object values that together comprise the JOSE Header.

requirements.condition: forming the JOSE Header from a JWE JSON Serialization's three header objects
requirements.behavior: reject the message when a Header Parameter name occurs in more than one of them
requirements.observable_effect: a message restating any parameter across two headers fails before any key is used
requirements.oracle: jwe.checkHeaders returns jwe.ErrDuplicateHeaderParameter for each of the three pairings -- protected against shared, protected against per-recipient, and shared against per-recipient -- and Decrypt calls it before any key management step. All three pairings are asserted, not only protected-against-the-rest: a name appearing in both unprotected headers and neither protected one is just as undefined, and is what a two-way check would miss. The security half is concrete: a kid or an epk restated outside the tag's coverage is a value an attacker can change without disturbing the tag. The check covers recipients this module cannot serve as well, reading their member names out of the octets their header arrived as (header.MembersIn). That is not tidiness: an unparsed per-recipient header is invisible to contentEncryption's own sweep for a stray "enc", so the disjointness check is the only thing standing between it and a second content encryption algorithm. It collides with the protected header's, which section 4.1.2 requires to be present (TestAnUnserviceableRecipientIsStillCheckedForDisjointness).
inputs: a message with kid in the protected and shared headers
and in the two unprotected headers

notes: contains a conditional; capture the guard in `condition` rather than in `behavior`

source.text: The CEK MUST have a length equal to that required for the content encryption algorithm.

requirements.condition: a CEK has been recovered by unwrapping the JWE Encrypted Key
requirements.behavior: reject it unless it is exactly the length the "enc" algorithm requires
requirements.observable_effect: an unwrap producing the wrong number of octets fails as an ordinary decryption failure
requirements.oracle: jwa.checkContentEncryptionKeySize returns jwa.ErrDecryptionFailed -- not ErrInvalidKeySize -- when a recovered CEK is the wrong length, and every DecryptKey calls it. The choice of error is the point and is asserted: on this path the length is a fact about the token, so an attacker able to tell "the unwrap succeeded but gave the wrong length" from "the unwrap failed" would have the beginnings of the oracle section 11.5 denies them. Exercised by wrapping a deliberately short key under A128KW and decrypting.
inputs: a JWE Encrypted Key wrapping a CEK of the wrong length

source.text: If there was no recipient for which all of the decryption steps succeeded, then the JWE MUST be considered invalid.

requirements.condition: no recipient completed every decryption step -- as distinct from some recipient not having done so
requirements.behavior: consider the JWE invalid
requirements.observable_effect: Decrypt returns an error and no plaintext; and DecryptAll returns, alongside them, one outcome per recipient saying which entry yielded the plaintext and which did not
requirements.oracle:
Decrypting with a wrong key, a tampered ciphertext, a tampered tag, a tampered IV or a tampered protected header each returns an error and a nil plaintext. No partial output is emitted on any path, which is the same rule step 16 states for the tag specifically.

The converse is asserted alongside it, and is the half that found a defect. The sentence says no recipient, not any recipient: steps 12 and 13 record per recipient whether the CEK could be determined and repeat the process for each, so a recipient that fails is an input to step 18 rather than an end to the procedure. Until this was implemented, jwe decoded each recipient's header into a header.Header, which refuses an unimplemented "alg" outright, so one entry naming an algorithm this module lacked failed the whole document -- making both this specification's own multi-recipient example (Appendix A.4) and RFC 7520 section 5.13 unreadable by a holder of the other recipients' keys. RSA1_5 was that algorithm in both, and is implemented now, so the case is exercised against A.4 with the first recipient's "alg" rewritten to a name no registry holds -- a producer using an algorithm a consumer lacks being the situation, not that one specific algorithm. A recipient this module cannot serve is now retained unparsed and recorded as failed; only jwa.ErrUnsupportedAlgorithm is treated that way, so a structurally malformed header is still a document that cannot be read (TestAMalformedRecipientHeaderIsStillFatal).

Step 18's second sentence -- "In the JWE JSON Serialization case, also return a result to the application indicating for which of the recipients the decryption succeeded and failed" -- is answered by jwe.Message.DecryptAll, which returns what Decrypt returns plus a []jwe.RecipientOutcome in the message's own recipient order. Asserted twice against Appendix A.4, because the vector now carries both halves of the boundary below. With the first recipient rewritten, decrypting under the A.3.3 octet key gives two outcomes, the rewritten entry failed and naming jwa.ErrUnsupportedAlgorithm, the A128KW entry succeeded and carrying the recipient whose header holds kid "7" (TestTheOutcomeOfEachRecipientIsReported). As published, both entries name algorithms this module implements, so the same key fails the RSA1_5 entry on the far side of the key instead, and that outcome says only jwa.ErrDecryptionFailed (TestTheOutcomeOfARecipientWeCouldNotOpenIsOpaque). RFC 7520 section 5.13 gives the assertion at width three under each of its three keys in turn, which shows the outcomes track the key rather than the document -- the entry that succeeds moves.

What an outcome may say is bounded by section 11.5 and is not a second rule: an "alg" that is absent or unimplementable is written in the document in plain sight, so it is named, and everything past that point -- an unwrap that failed, a tag that did not verify -- collapses to jwa.ErrDecryptionFailed exactly as it does for Decrypt. Telling those two apart is the decryption oracle section 11.5 exists to close, and a per-recipient report would be a fine place to reopen it.
inputs: a wrong key
each part tampered in turn
RFC 7516 Appendix A.4, whose two recipients are addressed with RSA1_5 and A128KW
the same document with the first recipient rewritten to an algorithm this module does not implement
RFC 7520 section 5.13, whose three recipients are addressed with three different key management algorithms
open_questions: Closed. This recorded step 18's second sentence as unimplemented: Decrypt returned the plaintext and an error with no per-recipient breakdown, so an application could not learn which entry it read. jwe.Message.DecryptAll now returns that breakdown. Decrypt is unchanged and still stops at the first recipient that works; DecryptAll attempts every one, which costs a key unwrap per remaining entry and is why the two are separate methods rather than one.

Not carried up to the token layer. jwt.Token decrypts through jwe.Message.Decrypt and exposes no per-recipient surface of its own. RFC 7519 asks for none, and a JWT addressed to several parties is a shape this module can read but has no API to describe; recorded here so the boundary is deliberate rather than overlooked.

notes: contains a conditional; capture the guard in `condition` rather than in `behavior`

source.text: Even if a JWE can be successfully decrypted, unless the algorithms used in the JWE are acceptable to the application, it SHOULD consider the JWE to be invalid.

requirements.condition: a JWE decrypts successfully but names algorithms the application has not permitted
requirements.behavior: consider the JWE invalid
requirements.observable_effect: decryption fails with a named error when alg or enc is outside the configured allowlist, even though the cryptography would have succeeded
requirements.oracle: jwt.Token.Decrypt checks both algorithms against DecryptionConfig's allowlists before using a key, returning jwt.ErrForbiddenKeyManagement or the enc equivalent. Configured with WithKeyManagementAlgorithms(jwa.A256KW()), a token encrypted with A128KW fails even though the key would unwrap it. The default allowlists exclude nothing this module implements, so the assertion is about the mechanism being reachable and effective, not about a particular policy -- which algorithms are acceptable is the application's decision, as the sentence says.
inputs: a token whose alg is outside the configured allowlist
the same for enc

notes: contains a conditional; capture the guard in `condition` rather than in `behavior`

source.text: The JWE Compact Serialization represents encrypted content as a compact, URL-safe string.  This string is: BASE64URL(UTF8(JWE Protected Header)) || '.' || BASE64URL(JWE Encrypted Key) || '.' || BASE64URL(JWE Initialization Vector) || '.' || BASE64URL(JWE Ciphertext) || '.' || BASE64URL(JWE Authentication Tag).

requirements.condition: producing or consuming the JWE Compact Serialization
requirements.behavior: use exactly those five base64url parts in that order, separated by four full stops
requirements.observable_effect: a compact JWE has five parts, and each decodes to the component the grammar names
requirements.oracle:
jwe.Message.Marshal produces a string with exactly four '.' characters, whose parts base64url-decode without padding to the protected header, encrypted key, IV, ciphertext and tag in that order; jwe.Unmarshal rejects any other count with jwe.ErrMalformedMessage. The ordering is checked against the RFC 7520 section 5 vectors rather than only against this module's own output, which is what makes it a test of the grammar rather than of self-consistency.

No BCP 14 keyword appears in this sentence. It is enriched anyway because it is the wire format: an implementation that ordered the parts differently would be unreadable by every other, and RFC 8174 section 2 says plainly that normative text need not use the keywords.
inputs: a compact JWE
strings with two, three and six parts
RFC 7520 section 5 vectors

notes: Added during enrichment. The sentence carries no BCP 14 keyword; RFC 8174 section 2 notes that much normative text does not, and this is wire format or security-critical behaviour rather than commentary.

source_review.reason: The prose is verbatim; the compact-serialization figure that follows is the section's displayed BASE64URL(...) || '.' || ... block joined onto one line, with the trailing period added to close the sentence.

source.text: Only one recipient is supported by the JWE Compact Serialization and it provides no syntax to represent JWE Shared Unprotected Header, JWE Per-Recipient Unprotected Header, or JWE AAD values.

requirements.condition: serializing a message compactly that has several recipients, an unprotected header or an aad
requirements.behavior: refuse, rather than serialize without them
requirements.observable_effect: Marshal fails instead of silently dropping values a recipient needs
requirements.oracle: jwe.Message.Marshal returns jwe.ErrMalformedMessage for a message with more than one recipient, with a non-empty shared unprotected header, with a non-empty per-recipient header, or with a non-nil aad. Refusing rather than dropping is the point: a compact serialization written without the aad would produce a different AAD on the way back and fail the tag check, reporting a cryptographic failure for what was a serialization mistake.
inputs: a two-recipient message
a message with a shared header
a message with an aad

notes: Added during enrichment. The sentence carries no BCP 14 keyword; RFC 8174 section 2 notes that much normative text does not, and this is wire format or security-critical behaviour rather than commentary.

source.text: protected The "protected" member MUST be present and contain the value BASE64URL(UTF8(JWE Protected Header)) when the JWE Protected Header value is non-empty; otherwise, it MUST be absent.

requirements.condition: serializing a JWE as JSON when the protected value is non-empty
requirements.behavior: write "protected" in the top-level object, carrying BASE64URL(UTF8(JWE Protected Header))
requirements.observable_effect: "protected" is present and holds the encoded value
requirements.oracle: json.Marshal of a jwe.Message with a non-empty protected value writes "protected" as BASE64URL(UTF8(JWE Protected Header)). Decoding the document back and decrypting recovers the plaintext, which is what makes the encoding assertion more than a string comparison: the value has to be the right one, not merely present.

source.text: protected The "protected" member MUST be present and contain the value BASE64URL(UTF8(JWE Protected Header)) when the JWE Protected Header value is non-empty; otherwise, it MUST be absent.

requirements.condition: serializing a JWE as JSON when the protected value is empty

requirements.observable_effect: the serialized object has no "protected" member at all

source.text: The JOSE Header for a JWS can also be distinguished from the JOSE Header for a JWE by determining whether an "enc" (encryption algorithm) member exists.  If the "enc" member exists, it is a JWE; otherwise, it is a JWS.

requirements.oracle:
This test and the segment-count test of RFC7516-S9-R01 must agree, and the requirement worth asserting is what happens when they do not. Both disagreement cases are refused, at different points, and the test asserts each where it actually happens rather than where it would be tidier:

A three-part token whose protected header carries an "enc" fails at jwt.Unmarshal with jws.ErrEncryptionAlgorithm. This was a real gap found while writing this suite: before the check was added, such a token parsed as a JWS and its signature verified normally, so a relying party using the segment-count rule would have trusted content that a relying party using the enc-member rule would have tried to decrypt.

A five-part token whose header names no "enc" parses -- the claims are unavailable until a key arrives, so nothing is decided yet -- and fails at Decrypt with jwe.ErrMalformedMessage. That is later but not weaker: no claim is readable and no plaintext is emitted in between.

Refusing rather than resolving is the point. The section's own caveat anticipates the case -- the methods may yield different results for malformed inputs -- and picking a winner would let a producer choose which rule a given consumer applied, which is the algorithm confusion of RFC 8725 section 3.1 arriving by a different route.

a five-part token whose header carries none

source.text: It is therefore particularly important to report all formatting errors to the CEK, Additional Authenticated Data, or ciphertext as a single error when the encrypted content is rejected.

requirements.condition: a JWE is rejected for any cryptographic reason
requirements.behavior: report one error covering the CEK, the AAD and the ciphertext alike

requirements.oracle:
See RFC7516-S11_5-R01, which carries the single-error assertion: every token-derived failure returns jwa.ErrDecryptionFailed. This entry records the attack that motivates it, and the countermeasures this module takes against it.

The attack was unreachable here by construction until RSA1_5 was implemented: rewriting alg to "RSA1_5" gave jwa.ErrUnsupportedAlgorithm before any key was touched. RSA1_5 decrypts now, so the paragraph applies to a real code path and three things close it instead. They are asserted in the order an attacker meets them, by TestRSA1_5IsNoDecryptionOracle.

First, the rewrite produces no formatting error to observe. jwa.RSAESPKCS1v15.DecryptKey substitutes a random CEK rather than reporting bad padding -- this section's own next paragraph, and RFC 3218's countermeasure -- so the rewritten token fails at the tag check with the same jwa.ErrDecryptionFailed a tampered ciphertext gives. The two error strings are compared directly, not merely matched against a sentinel.

Second, "alg" in the case the paragraph describes is in the JWE Protected Header, which is the Additional Authenticated Data, so the rewrite is itself tampering with the AAD and the tag would not verify even had the unwrap succeeded.

Third, the paragraph's own further countermeasure -- restricting a key to a limited set of algorithms, usually one -- is what jwk.Key's alg and key_ops members do and what DecryptionConfig's allowlists do at the token layer. RSA1_5 is not among the algorithms jwt.DefaultDecryptionConfig accepts, so the rewritten token is refused with jwt.ErrForbiddenKeyManagement before any key is touched unless a caller names the algorithm. See RFC8725-S3_2-R06.

No BCP 14 keyword appears here; the sentence says "particularly important". It is enriched because it is the concrete attack that section 11.5's MUST NOT exists to prevent.
inputs: a JWE whose alg has been rewritten from RSA-OAEP to RSA1_5

source.text: To mitigate the attacks described in RFC 3218 [RFC3218], the recipient MUST NOT distinguish between format, padding, and length errors of encrypted keys.

requirements.condition: an encrypted key fails to decrypt for any reason
requirements.behavior: not let the recipient distinguish format, padding and length errors from one another
requirements.observable_effect: every token-derived decryption failure returns the identical error value
requirements.oracle:
Every failure that depends on the token returns exactly jwa.ErrDecryptionFailed and nothing more specific: a tampered encrypted key, a tampered tag, a tampered IV, a tampered ciphertext, a tampered protected header, a wrapped CEK of the wrong length, and malformed CBC padding. Asserted with errors.Is against that single value across every alg and enc pairing, and by walking every octet of the tag rather than only the first -- a comparison checking a prefix would be caught by a flip at octet zero and by nothing else.

The boundary is deliberate and is stated rather than left implicit: failures that depend on the recipient's own key instead of on the token -- jwa.ErrInvalidKeyType, ErrInvalidKeySize, ErrWeakKey, ErrExcessiveIterationCount -- stay distinct, and are surfaced only when a single recipient makes attribution unambiguous. An attacker chooses none of those, and answering a caller's own mistake with "decryption failed" would trade a real diagnostic for no security.

The RFC's further recommendation -- substitute a random CEK and proceed -- is implemented for RSA1_5 and for no other algorithm. It is the algorithm the recommendation is written about: RFC 3218, which this section cites, is a document about PKCS #1 v1.5 alone, and the substitution is what makes offering RSAES-PKCS1-v1_5 decryption defensible at all. jwa.RSAESPKCS1v15.DecryptKey draws a CEK of the length the "enc" algorithm needs and lets crypto/rsa.DecryptPKCS1v15SessionKey overwrite it only when the padding is correct, so an improperly formatted key is neither an error nor a shorter code path; the failure surfaces one step later at the tag check. Asserted by TestRSA1_5SubstitutesARandomKey, which checks the two properties the message layer cannot show: two different encrypted keys give two different CEKs, and one encrypted key gives a different CEK each time. A substitution that was predictable, cached or derived from the ciphertext would be one an attacker could tell from a real key, which is the leak the standard library documents as defeating the mitigation.

Every other key management algorithm returns early instead, which leaves a timing difference between a key that unwraps and one that does not. The sentence calls the substitution strongly recommended rather than required, and a timing assertion in a Go test would be measuring the scheduler, so the remaining gap is recorded rather than closed.

One failure of RSA1_5 stays an error: an encrypted key that is not less than the modulus. The modulus is public, so every party can make that comparison, and nothing about the padding is in the answer. At the message layer it is jwa.ErrDecryptionFailed like everything else.

sections.title: Key Identification
sections.reason: Defined by reference to RFC 7515 section 6, with the identified key being "the public key to which the JWE was encrypted". Carries no keyword. Errata 7719 questions whether RFC 7515 section 6's justification -- that these parameters need not be integrity protected, since a changed key makes validation fail -- transfers to encryption, and the reporter could not supply a correction. The point is sound and is recorded rather than dismissed: the argument holds only for key-committing AEADs, and neither AES-GCM nor AES_CBC_HMAC_SHA2 is one, so a ciphertext crafted to decrypt under two keys is not excluded by the tag alone. It does not change what this module does -- a rewritten kid still makes decryption fail here -- but it does mean the RFC's stated reason is weaker than it reads.
